pages.text: Hans Christian Andersen was born in 1805 in Odense, Denmark, the son of a cobbler. He was a thin, awkward, long-limbed child who did not fit in anywhere. He left Odense for Copenhagen at the age of fourteen with almost nothing, determined to become famous. He did. By the time he died in 1875, he was one of the most celebrated writers in the world. His fairy tales have been translated into more languages than almost any other book except the Bible.

image.note: Illustration: a young Andersen walking a road with a small bundle, looking back at a town

pages.text: Unlike the Grimm brothers, who collected existing folk tales, Andersen invented most of his stories himself. He drew on folk traditions and his own experiences, but the stories are distinctly his: melancholy, tender, and full of outsiders who are misjudged, overlooked, or persecuted for being different. This is not a coincidence. Andersen was an outsider all his life: poor, ungainly, socially anxious, in love with people who did not love him back. He put all of that into his stories.

A duck hatched a clutch of eggs. All the ducklings were golden and pretty. The last egg to hatch produced a large, grey, awkward creature that none of the other ducks could explain. They mocked it, pecked it, and drove it away. It spent an entire year alone, surviving cold and hunger and cruelty, never understanding why it was different or what it was.

image.note: Illustration: a large grey cygnet standing apart from golden ducklings, head lowered

pages.text: In spring it came to a lake where three magnificent white birds were swimming. Expecting to be driven away as always, it flew toward them, willing to be killed rather than endure another winter alone. The three birds swam toward it. It looked down at its reflection in the water. It was no longer grey and awkward. It was a swan. It had always been a swan. It had spent its first year surrounded by ducks who could not understand what they were looking at.

Andersen wrote this story about himself. He knew what it was to be the wrong shape in the wrong place and to be made to feel worthless for it. He also knew, eventually, that the judgment of ducks is not the final word on the value of a swan.

A sea king's youngest daughter fell in love with a human prince she had seen from the water. She went to a sea witch who offered to give her legs, in exchange for her voice, the most beautiful in the sea. Every step she took on her new legs felt like walking on knives. The prince never knew she loved him. He married a human princess.

image.note: Illustration: the little mermaid sitting on a rock at sunset, watching a distant ship

pages.text: In Andersen's original story, the little mermaid does not get a happy ending. She is offered the chance to save herself by killing the prince. She cannot do it. At dawn she dissolves into sea foam. In later editions, Andersen gave her a slightly gentler fate: she becomes a spirit of the air and, through centuries of good deeds, earns a soul and entry into heaven. It is still not the ending she wanted.

The story is often read as Andersen's account of unrequited love: the experience of loving someone who does not see you, of transforming yourself for their sake, and of still not being enough. It is a painful story. It is also, for that reason, one of the most widely recognised in the world.

Andersen wrote another tale that children have loved and shivered at for generations. A little match girl, barefoot and freezing on the last night of the year, dares not go home because she has sold no matches, and her father will beat her. To warm her hands she strikes the matches one by one, and in each small flame she sees a vision: a warm stove, a feast, a bright tree, and at last her beloved grandmother, the only person who was ever kind to her.

In the morning she is found still and cold, the burnt matches beside her, a smile on her face. It is one of the saddest stories ever written for children, and Andersen meant it to be. He had known real hunger and real cold, and he refused to pretend they did not exist. Yet he gives the child, in her last moments, the one thing she longed for. Andersen's mercy is never cheap, but it is always there.

A devil made a mirror that distorted everything good and beautiful into something ugly and ridiculous. The mirror shattered, and its splinters flew into people's eyes and hearts, making them cold and cruel. A splinter entered the eye of a boy named Kay, and he became unkind, seeing only the flaws in everything. The Snow Queen came and took him to her palace of ice.

image.note: Illustration: the Snow Queen in her sleigh carrying a small boy, an icy palace visible in the distance

pages.text: Kay's friend Gerda set out to find him, travelling through dangers that would have defeated most adults: a witch's garden, a robber band, a reindeer crossing a frozen wilderness. She reached the Snow Queen's palace and found Kay, alone, trying to spell a word in ice. Gerda wept over him, and her hot tears melted the splinter from his eye.

The Snow Queen is Andersen's longest and most complex story. Its message is simple: clever determination driven by love can do what armies and magic cannot. Gerda has no weapons, no magic, and no power. She simply will not stop.

What Andersen gave to the world was not only stories but a particular quality of compassion: an unflinching willingness to look at pain and loneliness directly, to give them form in a story, and to find in them something true.

image.note: Illustration: children in a library, books open, absorbed in reading

pages.text: The ugly duckling, the little mermaid, the steadfast tin soldier: all of Andersen's most memorable characters are people or creatures who do not quite fit, who suffer because of it, and who endure. Not all of them get happy endings. Some die. Some dissolve into sea foam. Some burn on a grate. But none of them give up their nature to be comfortable. None of them pretend to be something they are not.

That is, perhaps, the real lesson in all of Andersen's tales: be what you are, even when it hurts. What you are may matter more than you know. And even if no one recognises it in your lifetime, you were still a swan.

Andersen also wrote comedy, and one tale still makes people laugh at their own foolishness. Two swindlers convince an emperor they can weave cloth so fine that only the wise can see it, and so beautiful that fools see nothing at all. Terrified of seeming foolish, the emperor, his ministers, and his whole city praise the invisible cloth, until the emperor parades through the streets wearing nothing but his own vanity, and every adult applauds the splendid robes.

Then a small child, too young to have learned to pretend, says out loud: but he has nothing on. And the spell breaks. It is Andersen's sharpest tale: a whole society agreeing to a lie because each person is afraid to be the one who admits the truth, undone at last by a child honest enough to say what everyone can see. Two centuries on, the emperor's new clothes remain the perfect name for a fashionable nonsense that no one dares to question.
